Photograph: Nordin Catic/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A vigil for Jason Arday was held outside the University of Cambridge’s Senate House building on Sunday. Photograph: Nordin Catic/Getty Images Jason Arday Support for Jason Arday’s family shows ‘Britain still cares’, says Windrush campaigner Crowdfund passes £150,000, while Cambridge chancellor criticises ‘racist feeding frenzy’ around academic’s death Press Association Mon 17 Aug 2026 08.02 EDT Last modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 08.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Windrush campaigner who launched a fundraiser for Jason Arday’s family has said the outpouring of support shows “Britain still cares”. Arday, who was found dead on Friday , had resigned the previous week from his post as professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge after allegations of plagiarism were made against him. A vigil organised by the group Stand Up to Racism will be held on the steps of the National Gallery in Trafalgar Square, central London, at 6pm on Monday. Cambridge’s chancellor, Chris Smith, has broken his silence over the controversy and described a “racist feeding frenzy” around the academic’s death. View image in fullscreen Students and staff left tributes to Arday at the gates of the Senate House in Cambridge on Friday. Photograph: Nordin Catic/Getty Images On Saturday, Sir Patrick Vernon, who played a leading role in the successful campaign to establish a national Windrush Day, set up a GoFundMe crowdfunding page, which has collected more than £150,000. He told the Press Association the outpouring of support shows that the public “still cares” and felt “angry”. “Britain still cares – people, black, white, brown, care and feel angry about the situation,” he said. “People want to support the family. There’s lots of speculation about how much money Jason has or doesn’t have – that’s not the point. The fact is, people want to support the family because he’s dead, he’s died and he has a young family. “He has parents and he has a family that he has supported, and people want to support the family.” Cambridge University defends its mental health support for Jason Arday Read more Vernon was one of several public figures, including the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, and the crossbench peer Simon Woolley, to sign an open letter supporting Arday as he faced mounting scrutiny from the press. Vernon said the treatment of Arday raised questions around press regulation, the University of Cambridge and the “state of race relations in Britain today”. Before Arday’s death, Cambridge said it would investigate the circumstances around his “appointment and tenure” and the findings would feed into a review of the process for appointing senior roles. It is understood the university does not feel it is right to make a decision on whether to proceed with its investigation while Arday’s family are grieving. In a statement released on Monday, Smith said: “I do believe it is possible to hold to two principles at the same time: to believe in the importance of academic integrity, and where criticisms of plagiarism arise, about any academic, whoever they are, ensure that they are rigorously investigated. And also to refuse to join in a racist feeding frenzy over a particular academic.” Downing Street declined to say “at this stage” whether Andy Burnham was considering an inquiry over the death of Arday. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy decries ‘absolutely unjust’ lack of warning from allies after Kyiv plant strike Donald Trump has denied intelligence sharing with Ukraine had stopped, while demanding that Kyiv halts strikes on Russian refineries. What we know on day 1,694 Guardian staff and agencies Tue 13 Oct 2026 21.04 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Russian ballistic missile struck a power plant in Kyiv on Tuesday evening without Ukraine receiving advance warning from its western allies , Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The president said Ukraine’s systems picked up the missiles only as they were nearing the city. “This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches,” he added. US officials made explicit threats over the weekend to their Ukrainian counterparts that the Trump administration was on the brink of halting intelligence sharing with Kyiv. Donald Trump has denied intelligence sharing had stopped , telling reporters on Tuesday: “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we’re working with them and Russia on getting the war to end.” Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries and has blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in fuel prices in the US. On Friday the US president announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia, dropping previous US sanctions. Two people also died in a strike on a high-rise apartment building in the capital on Tuesday night , according to Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko, who said apartments were on fire and being evacuated. A further 21 injuries were reported. Emergency ‌crews were battling fires in apartments throughout the building and residents were being ‌evacuated. Zelenskyy has said he has proposed new talks with ⁠US ​envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The proposal follows talks in ​the US last week ‌at which Witkoff and Kushner told ‌a Ukrainian delegation that a deal allowing Russian diesel exports was aimed at drawing Moscow back to negotiations. In a video ‌address on Tuesday night, Zelenskyy also reiterated that Ukraine supported president Donald Trump’s proposed ​energy truce as long as Russia observed it. “Our team has sent the American side the ⁠relevant proposals regarding possible next meetings and ​conversations,” he said. Trump is facing cross-party calls on Capitol Hill to ditch his controversial diesel deal with Russia . A group of six Republican and six Democrat senators has jointly warned that the lifting of sanctions to allow Moscow to sell the fuel is “a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies”. The US president has defended the decision as he seeks to increase supply and so bring down soaring pump prices ahead of critical stateside elections next month, which will decide control of Congress. The EU has opened new areas of negotiations with Ukraine, marking a key step in Kyiv’s long path to join the bloc. Ukraine took a step forward in ⁠its membership bid on Tuesday, opening talks ⁠on ​internal market and competitiveness standards, Irish minister of state for ⁠European affairs Thomas Byrne said, after Hungary dropped its objections. The move came after Ukrainian lawmakers passed legislation protecting the rights of the Hungarian-speaking minority in western Ukraine, which has long caused tensions with Budapest. Hungary had blocked Ukraine’s EU membership bid, officially submitted days after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. Suspected Russian drones struck two cargo ships off Bulgaria on Tuesday, sinking one vessel and leaving 11 sailors missing in the latest spillover from the Ukraine war in the Black Sea. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev summoned the Russian ambassador after drones struck a Ukrainian-owned cargo ship, the Chelsea 3, while another vessel, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship Dignity, was also hit and sank farther north off the coast. Radev called the attacks “absolutely unacceptable” and said Bulgaria was seeking Nato and EU assistance. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen called the attacks “another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine”. The Russian Defence Ministry on Tuesday said its air defences overnight shot down 604 Ukrainian drones across the country and the Sea of Azov. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 417 drones targeted the Moscow region. Most were downed far away, while 65 were intercepted as they approached the Russian capital. A school, two private houses and a car were damaged in the attack in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow, governor Vladislav Shapsha said. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3vg.text: Image source, Reuters By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 30 October 2026 Updated 2 hours ago The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks. However Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned it could take "several years" for the deliveries to arrive. The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (Â£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada. On Friday night Zelensky repeated his calls for the US to speed up the release of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles. Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire Published 11 hours ago G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister Published 5 hours ago The latest move comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel. The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east. Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October. In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe". It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan". The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale". Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph. The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine. Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies which his country was running critically low on. In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now". He said Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks. Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran. It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine. Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence. In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriots - three weeks after offering the country such a right.
